title: Hot for its bot, McKinsey may cut thousands of jobs
author: O'Ryan Johnson

kp.k: McKinsey reportedly considers thousands of support-role cuts
kp.d: The Register's 16 December 2025 article reports Bloomberg's account that McKinsey was considering a few thousand job cuts over the next 18 to 24 months, with reductions of up to 10 percent discussed for some non-client-facing teams. McKinsey's spokesperson linked support-function reform to efficiency amid rapid AI advances, but did not confirm the number of cuts or identify AI as the sole cause. McKinsey did not respond to The Register's requests for comment.
qs: The spokesperson would not confirm the number of cuts nor did they say that AI was the only cause.

But Bloomberg, which first broke the story of layoffs, said the cuts could be staggered over the next 18 to 24 months and amount to a few thousand roles, with reductions of up to 10 percent discussed for some non-client-facing teams.
Just as we're partnering with clients to strengthen their organizations, we're on our own journey to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of our support functions.

kp.k: Reported AI labour-market findings and forecasts conflict
kp.d: The article juxtaposes a Yale study reporting zero effect on jobs, a US Senate report estimating potential elimination of 97 million positions, and a BearingPoint survey of 1,000 executives in which roughly half reported 10–19 percent workforce overcapacity as AI automation rolls out. These are presented as conflicting accounts, not as a settled estimate of AI-driven job losses.
qs: There have been several conflicting reports this year about how AI is shaping the labor market with a Yale study that found zero effect on jobs, a report from the US Senate that estimated it could eliminate 97 million positions, and a BearingPoint survey of 1,000 execs in which roughly half reported 10–19 percent workforce overcapacity as AI-driven automation is rolled out.

kp.k: Consulting firms deploy internally adopted AI assistants
kp.d: Citing a September Harvard Business Review report, the article describes adoption of internal assistants across McKinsey, Bain, KPMG, Boston Consulting Group and PwC. It identifies Lilli, Sage, KymChat, Deckster and ChatPwC respectively, specifying that Deckster creates slide presentations. The discussion concerns consulting operations rather than legal-service delivery.
qs: As AI prompts a reckoning among enterprise customers, consulting firms like McKinsey, Bain, KPMG, Boston Consulting Group, and PricewaterhouseCoopers have each deployed internal bot assistants that are winning adoption, according to the Harvard Business Review, which looked at how AI would shape this industry in a September report.
McKinsey has "Lilli," Bain has "Sage," PwC has "ChatPwC," and KPMG uses "KymChat," while Boston Consulting Group uses "Deckster" to create slide presentations.

kp.k: Lilli reportedly reduces information-search and synthesis time
kp.d: Internal assessments suggest McKinsey's Lilli can reduce time spent searching for and synthesizing information by up to 30 percent. A McKinsey case study from the preceding September describes it drawing on dozens of internal knowledge sources to retrieve material and generate answers previously requiring substantial manual research. The reported measure is task-time reduction, not a quantified headcount effect.
qs: Internal assessments suggest Lilli can cut time spent searching for and synthesizing information by up to 30 percent.

The tool acts as a synthesis engine, drawing on dozens of internal knowledge sources to surface relevant material and generate answers that previously required significant manual research, McKinsey stated in a case study last September.

kp.k: AI reshapes consulting pyramids into leaner obelisks
kp.d: The article describes a shift from pyramid staffing to an obelisk with fewer employees at every level. The HBR piece anticipates smaller groups of early-career AI facilitators replacing a large base of junior MBAs, progressing to engagement architects who lead projects and interpret AI outputs, and subsequently to client leaders managing relationships. This is a proposed trajectory for consulting roles and staffing, rather than a measured outcome presented in the article.
qs: The emergence of AI as well as the internal tools are reshaping the organization from a pyramid structure to an obelisk, with fewer employees at every level.

Instead of a large base of junior MBAs, there will be smaller groups of early-career AI facilitators, who will become engagement architects who lead projects and interpret AI outputs, and then client leaders who manage relationships with clients, the Harvard Business Review piece states.

kp.k: Competitive advantage requires redesigning workflows around AI
kp.d: HBR coauthor Jeffrey Saviano recommends that consulting firms move quickly to rebuild around AI-embedded workflows. In a LinkedIn post promoting the report, he predicts success for leaner, expert-driven and responsibly governed models rather than firms simply adding AI to existing pyramid structures.
qs: One of the report's authors, Jeffrey Saviano, who spent 30 years at Ernst & Young, said consultants need to move quickly to rearchitect their firms around workflows where AI is embedded.
The winners won't be those who merely bolt AI onto an old pyramid. They will be those who reimagine the model entirely: leaner, more expert-driven, and governed with responsibility,

kp.k: Consulting contraction may reflect declining traditional strategy demand
kp.d: Recruitment-firm CEO James O'Dowd characterises McKinsey's move as strategic and estimates its headcount of 36,000 is already down 25 percent from peak levels, not necessarily because of AI. He argues that demand for traditional strategy consulting is structurally declining as boards favour technology-fluent builder-CEOs and place greater weight on execution, monetization and measurable impact than on abstract frameworks and top-down transformation plans.
qs: He estimates the McKinsey headcount at 36,000 is already down 25 percent from peak levels and not necessarily because of AI.

The uncomfortable reality is that demand for traditional strategy consulting is structurally declining. Boards are hiring builder-CEOs with genuine technology fluency, product instincts and the ability to execute at speed,
Abstract frameworks and top-down transformation playbooks carry less weight when delivery, monetization and measurable impact have become the true currency of value.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article reports prospective consulting-sector job cuts, research-efficiency gains and a predicted move toward leaner, AI-integrated staffing structures. These are consulting claims, not claims about legal services.
pts.d: O'Ryan Johnson frames McKinsey's reported consideration of thousands of job cuts as occurring amid AI advances and an efficiency drive, rather than establishing AI as their sole cause. Bloomberg is identified as the source for the prospective cut figures. McKinsey's internal assessment claims that Lilli reduces time spent searching for and synthesizing information by up to 30 percent. The September Harvard Business Review piece, as described by Johnson, predicts a shift from a pyramid to an 'obelisk': fewer employees at every level, smaller entry-level cohorts working as AI facilitators, progression into engagement architects interpreting AI outputs and leading projects, and client leaders managing relationships. HBR co-author Jeffrey Saviano argues that successful firms will redesign workflows around AI rather than add it to existing staffing models. James O'Dowd offers a qualification: he characterizes McKinsey's move as strategic and attributes pressure on traditional strategy consulting to declining demand and a preference for execution capability, not necessarily AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of attributed reporting, company internal assessments, an HBR industry analysis and practitioner commentary; the article also recounts conflicting broader labor-market findings.
pts.d: The proposed layoff scale comes from Bloomberg reporting, not a confirmed McKinsey announcement. A McKinsey spokesperson confirms an efficiency initiative concerning support functions but does not confirm cut numbers or exclusive AI causation. The Lilli productivity figure comes from internal assessments, alongside a McKinsey case study describing synthesis across dozens of internal knowledge sources; no assessment methodology or independent validation is supplied. HBR supplies the account of internal assistant adoption and the future staffing model. Named tools include McKinsey's Lilli, Bain's Sage, PwC's ChatPwC, KPMG's KymChat and BCG's slide-making Deckster. Saviano's argument is practitioner commentary, with 30 years at Ernst & Young cited as background. O'Dowd, a professional-services recruiter, estimates that McKinsey's headcount of 36,000 is already 25 percent below peak, without a supporting data series in the article. As contextual evidence rather than proof of McKinsey-specific causation, Johnson contrasts a Yale study reported to find no job effects, a US Senate estimate of 97 million potential job eliminations, and a BearingPoint survey of 1,000 executives reporting workforce overcapacity. The article provides no detailed methods or projection horizon for those broader findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The contemplated cuts extend over 18–24 months from the December 2025 reporting; productivity gains are presented as current internal findings, while the staffing transformation has no firm completion date.
pts.d: The article is dated 16 December 2025. Bloomberg's reported cuts are prospective, could be staggered over the following 18–24 months and remain under discussion. The 'up to 10 percent' figure applies to some non-client-facing teams, not the entire firm. Lilli's 'up to 30 percent' improvement concerns searching for and synthesizing information, not all consulting work or total staffing requirements. The HBR analysis and McKinsey case study are described as September publications. The staffing redesign is framed as emerging and future-facing, without a quantified transition timetable. Saviano conditions competitive success on rapid redesign of AI-embedded workflows and responsible governance. O'Dowd explicitly cautions that the already-reduced headcount is not necessarily attributable to AI; no date for the headcount peak is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are consulting support staff, junior recruits, project leaders and client-relationship leaders, with broader implications for advisory firms and their enterprise clients.
pts.d: McKinsey support functions and some non-client-facing teams face the reported prospective reductions. Consultants using internal assistants are described as gaining faster access to synthesized institutional knowledge. The predicted organizational model reduces staffing at every level, especially the large junior-MBA base, while redefining career roles around AI facilitation, project architecture, interpretation of AI outputs and client relationships. McKinsey, Bain, KPMG, BCG and PwC are discussed as consulting organizations deploying assistants; the article does not make claims about their legal-services operations. Saviano's argument concerns which consulting firms will succeed through organizational redesign. O'Dowd describes corporate boards as shifting demand toward technology-fluent, execution-oriented leaders and away from traditional strategy frameworks. The broader labor-market studies concern workers and enterprise workforces generally, rather than a specified legal or consulting-only population.
